facts.text: Machine Performance Level (MPL) is the earth-moving-machinery version of Performance Level, defined in the ISO 19014 series; hazard analysis sets the required level (MPLr), and the design demonstrates the achieved level (MPLa).
facts.quote: The Machine Performance Level is the earth-moving-machinery version of the Performance Level, defined in the ISO 19014 series, with a required level (MPLr) set by hazard analysis and an achieved level (MPLa) demonstrated by the design.

facts.text: Machine Performance Level follows the Performance Level concept of ISO 13849, tailored to loaders, haul trucks and excavators, and uses levels a to e.
facts.quote: The idea is the same as the Performance Level of ISO 13849, tailored to loaders, haul trucks and excavators, and the levels use the same lettering, a to e.

facts.text: ISO 19014-1 provides Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA), the method for identifying safety-related parts of the control system and setting the required Machine Performance Level.
facts.quote: ISO 19014-1 gives the method, the Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA), which finds the safety-related parts of the control system and sets the required level.

facts.text: ISO 19014-2 covers hardware and architecture and gives the achieved Machine Performance Level.
facts.quote: ISO 19014-2 covers hardware and architecture and gives the achieved level.

facts.text: ISO 19014-3 sets environmental tests for machine-control electronics.
facts.quote: Part 3 sets environmental tests for the electronics

facts.text: ISO 19014-4 covers software and data transmission.
facts.quote: Part 4 covers software and data transmission

facts.text: ISO 19014-5 provides tables of required Machine Performance Levels for common machine functions; manufacturers can use a tabulated value without a full MCSSA for each new model when the table's assumptions hold.
facts.quote: Part 5 is a set of tables of required levels for common machine functions, so a manufacturer can apply a tabulated value "without performing a full MCSSA for each new model" when the assumptions behind the table hold

facts.text: The booklet reports that second editions of ISO 19014 Parts 1 to 4 and a first full edition of Part 5 were all under publication for October 2026.
facts.quote: second editions of Parts 1 to 4 and a first full edition of Part 5 were all under publication for October 2026

facts.text: The booklet did not find a published required Machine Performance Level for collision avoidance or automatic braking.
facts.quote: A published required level for collision avoidance or automatic braking was not found

facts.text: The booklet did not review whether ISO 19014-5 tables contain a required Machine Performance Level for collision avoidance or automatic braking.
facts.quote: whether the Part 5 tables contain one was not reviewed

facts.text: The Machine Performance Level scale is not the Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL) scale used for road vehicles.
facts.quote: The MPL scale is not the ASIL scale of road vehicles

facts.text: The functional safety engineer in the hostile review calls for allocated Machine Performance Levels for both failure to intervene and incorrect intervention, mapped to the October 2026 ISO 19014 editions.
facts.quote: The functional safety engineer in the hostile review wants allocated levels for both failure to intervene and incorrect intervention, mapped to the October 2026 editions

facts.text: The required Machine Performance Level determines how much redundancy, diagnostics and evidence the braking chain needs.
facts.quote: The required MPL decides how much redundancy, diagnostics and evidence the braking chain needs.

facts.text: Leaving performance-level allocation undecided in 2027 is an early warning sign of a failing automatic-braking program.
facts.quote: Leaving "performance-level allocation" undecided in 2027 is an early warning sign of a failing program
